title: Validation rules; creating a data dictionary

learning_objectives.text: create a data dictionary for database tables

lesson_objectives.all: name the validation checks and choose a suitable data type for a field
lesson_objectives.most: write a complete data dictionary entry with a validation rule that fits the data and explain the difference between validation and verification
lesson_objectives.some: create a data dictionary for a whole table and choose normal, boundary and erroneous test data for its rules

descriptors: names presence, range, type, length, format, lookup and uniqueness checks
chooses a check that matches the data of a field
decides whether a value is accepted or rejected by a rule
explains that validation checks data is sensible, verification that it was copied correctly
names double entry and visual check
chooses data types and sizes for every field
marks primary and foreign keys; a foreign key has the same type as its primary key
writes a validation rule, a description and an example consistent with the rule

learners_can: state a rule precisely (The value must be …)
explain a choice with because / so that
compare two processes (Validation checks …, whereas verification …)
phrases: The rule for … is … , so the value … is rejected.
Boundary data for this rule is …

values.action: Learners review the topics of the term on their own in the written worksheet, find their gaps and plan what to revise.
Learners write validation rules carefully and check that every example passes its own rule, as accurate database designers do.
Partners compare their own ERDs, agree on the best one, build the data dictionary together and defend it in front of the class.

cross_curricular: English: writing precise rules and comparing two processes.
Mathematics: ranges, inequalities and boundary values; decimal places.
Biology / medicine and business: why data in clinics and shops must be validated.
ict: ICT Practice Platform, Lessons section: theory as slides, live votes and tasks, random pairs and client cards on the learners' screens.
Interactive validation checker in the theory: learners test a record against the rules.
Practice questions with automatic feedback; results visible to the teacher live.
previous_learning: Basic concepts of a database (tables, records, fields, data types, keys); entity-relationship diagrams; lesson 1 of this topic: what a data dictionary is, the items it records and its purpose.
safety: During the worksheet laptops stay closed.
Move to the group's laptop calmly; keep bags and cables off the floor.

support: The worksheet goes from recall to explanation; key words are given in the questions.
Worked example on the slides: the sports centre table and its data dictionary.
Client cards on the screens describe the entities; the sports centre worked example on the slides shows a complete data dictionary.
Random mixed-ability pairs; each learner draws an ERD first, so both take part before choosing one.
stretch: Write the SQL CREATE TABLE statements with CHECK and NOT NULL for the pair's tables.
Explain why a lookup check is unsuitable for 8 000 book titles.
Find a value that passes every check but is still wrong, and suggest how verification would catch it.

assessment: Written review worksheet (30 marks) marked by the teacher with the mark scheme; common gaps are discussed in the next lesson.
Live results of every task on the teacher's slide; misconceptions are discussed at once.
Pair project on paper (ERD, data dictionary with validation rules) assessed during the defence against the criteria; peers ask questions.
Exit ticket (marked automatically) checks the lesson objectives.
Practice results count towards SAU points.

blocks.title: Written review worksheet: term 2 so far
blocks.teacher: Greets the class, gives out the printed worksheet (databases, keys, ERD, data dictionary) and states the time: 30 minutes, written answers, no laptops. Walks round and notes common gaps. Collects the worksheets for marking with the mark scheme.
blocks.learners: Answer the worksheet questions in writing on their own.

blocks.title: Hook: Age = 150
blocks.teacher: Shows the objectives. Asks: a form saved a pupil with Age = 150. What should have stopped it? Learners vote; leads to validation rules.

poll.question: A school form saved a pupil with Age = 150. What should have stopped it?

resources: Title slide: objectives and key words

blocks.title: Slides: validation checks
blocks.teacher: Presents validation, the seven checks with accepted and rejected values, the validation checker, choosing a check, validation and verification, test data. Together tasks: which check is "size S, M, L or XL"? What happens to 78 typed instead of 87?
blocks.learners: Follow the slides, vote in the together tasks and suggest values that are accepted or rejected.
resources: Theory: Validation in a data dictionary (slides, interactive checker)

blocks.title: Pair work: checks, verification and test data
blocks.teacher: Opens the pair task: random pairs, one laptop each. Monitors live results and helps pairs that are stuck.
blocks.learners: In random pairs on one laptop: six practice questions on validation checks, verification and test data.

blocks.title: Slides: creating a data dictionary
blocks.teacher: Presents the steps, choosing data types and sizes, matching keys and the sports centre worked example. Together task: which type for an ISBN?
blocks.learners: Follow the worked example and vote.

blocks.title: Pair project: ERD → choose one → data dictionary
blocks.teacher: Forms random pairs; each pair gets a client card on the learners' screens. Step 1 (4 min): each learner draws the ERD alone on paper. Step 2 (3 min): partners compare the two ERDs — entities, degrees, link table for M:M — and choose the better one or merge them. Step 3 (13 min): together they write the data dictionary for every table of the chosen ERD on paper: field name, data type, size, key (PK / FK), validation rule, example. Checks that every field has a validation rule, foreign keys match their primary keys and every example passes its own rule.
blocks.learners: Draw the ERD on your own, compare with your partner and choose one, then write the data dictionary for all its tables with a validation rule for every field.
resources: Client cards on the learners' screens
Theory slide: a complete data dictionary (sports centre example)

blocks.title: Defence: pairs present to the class
blocks.teacher: Pairs present their ERD and data dictionary in turn (about 1 minute each, under the document camera or held up). The class asks one question to each pair (Why VARCHAR? Which check rejects …? Is the M:M resolved?). Teacher assesses with the criteria: ERD correct with M:M resolved; suitable types and sizes; keys match; a validation rule for every field; examples pass their rules; clear defence.
blocks.learners: Present and defend the pair's ERD and data dictionary; ask other pairs questions.

blocks.title: Exit ticket and homework
blocks.teacher: Opens the exit ticket. Homework: finish the remaining lesson 2 practice and hand in handwritten notes for lesson 2.
blocks.learners: Answer three questions and note the homework.

dd-l2-pairs.details: Patients and doctors. A patient can book many appointments; each appointment is with one doctor and one patient on a date and time. A doctor has many appointments. Store the patient's IIN (12 digits), name, date of birth and phone; the doctor's name and speciality.

Students and books. A student can borrow many books and a book can be borrowed by many students over time. Store each loan's date and return date; the student's ID (S + 4 digits), name and grade (11 or 12); the book's ISBN, title and number of copies.

Customers, orders and products. A customer places many orders; an order contains many products and a product is in many orders, each with a quantity. Store prices in tenge, order dates and the customer's e-mail.

Members and classes. A member attends many classes and a class has many members; each class has one trainer. Store the member's number (M + 4 digits), date of birth (at least 10 years old), the class name, day and maximum size (5–30).

Drivers, cars and trips. A driver makes many trips; each trip uses one car; a car is used for many trips. Store the car's number plate, the trip's distance in km (e.g. 12.4), fare in tenge and start time, and whether it was paid by card.

live_tasks.title: Which check?
live_tasks.text: The rule is: **T-shirt size must be S, M, L or XL**. Which validation check is it?

scheme.explanation: The value must be in a short list of allowed values.

live_tasks.title: Sensible but wrong
live_tasks.text: A teacher types the mark **78** instead of **87**. The rule is 0–100. What happens?

options.content: It is accepted — validation cannot tell it is wrong; verification is needed

scheme.explanation: Validation checks that data is sensible, not that it is correct.

live_tasks.title: Type for ISBN
live_tasks.text: An ISBN looks like `9786010000017` (13 digits, may start with 0, never used in calculations). Which data type should the data dictionary give it?

scheme.explanation: Codes that are not used in calculations — and may have leading zeros — are stored as text.

options.content: Pupil ID must be S followed by 4 digits

live_tasks.title: Double entry
live_tasks.text: Typing a password twice when you create an account is an example of …

scheme.explanation: The two entries are compared, so it checks that the data was entered correctly.

live_tasks.title: Price
live_tasks.text: Which data dictionary entry is correct for `Price` (in tenge, e.g. 4990.50)?

scheme.explanation: Money has a fractional part, so DECIMAL; a price must be more than 0.
